source.title: Gaussian Pre-Activations in Neural Networks: Myth or Reality?

record.tranche_reason: The study trains networks with different activation and initialization setups and reports training-loss outcomes bearing on trainability, using a different task and measure from the claim versions.
record.gate_note: Training-loss curves and explicit training descriptions bear on trainability. The study does not report training classification error, so it does not test V1's near-zero-error claim. Initialization and activation are paired in the proposed setup; their individual effects cannot be separated. Gaussianity and correlation measurements are not rows because they do not measure the claim's training outcome.
record.test_reason: The paired activation and initialization experiments measure training speed and attained loss in new settings, bearing on V4. They do not test V3's depth degradation in batch-normalized convolutional networks or its shortcut remedy.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly accurate. The authors tentatively associate Gaussian pre-activations combined with odd activations with trainability, but leave Gaussianity's desirability unresolved. Positive activations preserve Gaussianity better yet often train poorly in narrow, deep perceptrons; odd-pair outcomes depend on the parameter and architecture. Competitive LeNet training losses can accompany poorer generalization.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains networks with Adam and compares standard tanh or ReLU with newly designed activation functions paired with symmetric Weibull initialization. It does not reproduce the original studies' initialization or shortcut interventions.
record.method_sensitivity: Training outcomes vary by activation family, width, and depth; positive proposed activations are described as much harder to train than odd ones in narrow, deep networks.

fits_no_version.finding: Narrow, deep ReLU perceptrons are difficult to train.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Training difficulty in narrow multilayer perceptrons depends on activation choice.

fits_no_version.finding: Positive activations preserve approximately Gaussian pre-activations more reliably than odd ones, yet are harder to train in narrow, deep perceptrons.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Approximately Gaussian pre-activations alone do not guarantee successful training.

fits_no_version.finding: Some proposed LeNet configurations achieve competitive training loss but poorer test accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Activation and initialization choices that permit optimization need not provide equally good generalization.

record.problems: Training outcomes are shown as figures rather than numerical training-loss values in the text, and no training classification error is reported. In the proposed setup, activation function and initialization are paired, so their individual effects cannot be separated. The paper reports training curves averaged over 5 experiments but no uncertainty intervals.
record.rows_left_out: No additional training-loss results omitted. Gaussianity, correlation-propagation, and test-accuracy findings were not extracted as rows because they do not measure the training outcome named by the claim versions.

untested.parts: No training classification-error result establishing interpolation, random-label experiment, or CIFAR-100 experiment.
No ReLU teacher-student experiment or measurement of spurious minima versus excess student width.
No depth comparison of batch-normalized plain convolutional networks, identity-shortcut intervention, or very deep plain tanh/Fixup experiment.

Initialization is not isolated from activation choice. The experiments do not establish that gradient preservation causes the training advantage, compare orthogonal with Gaussian weights of equal variance, or test 10,000-layer convolutional networks.
No stability-threshold, curvature, sharpness, catapult, or edge-of-stability training experiment.
No normalization intervention or Fixup comparison.

missing.what: Positive activation and Weibull initialization training results: worse training than odd pairs in narrow perceptrons, with many failures at depth 30. These results contradict the record's assertion that no additional training-loss results were omitted.

Parameter-dependent outcomes within odd activation pairs: theta=2.05 can train LeNet well but may fail in narrow, deep perceptrons, whereas theta=10 shows the opposite pattern. R1's aggregate description conceals this qualification.
missing.locator: Section 6, discussion of whether Gaussian pre-activations are desirable; Figures 9 and 10

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source listed for these versions. Remove the proposed V3 verdict and the V4 generalization-cost verdict: neither follows from the corresponding claim. Gaussianity and correlation results concern initialization properties rather than direct measurements of training speed or trainable depth. Exact curve values cannot be recovered from the supplied text.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not report training classification error, zero or near-zero error, corrupted or random labels, CIFAR-100, or comparisons of model size and early stopping on training error.
No two-layer ReLU teacher-student problem, spurious-minimum frequency, or student-versus-teacher width comparison.
No residual shortcuts or batch-normalized plain-versus-residual comparison; no ImageNet experiment. Training outcomes are reported as loss, not training classification error.
The study does not test Glorot, He, or orthogonal initialization, nor does it isolate initialization from activation choice. No 10,000-layer convolutional network is tested.
No learning-rate stability threshold, sharpness, curvature, catapult phase, or divergence comparison.
No batch-normalization comparison or test of Fixup.

rows.subject: multilayer perceptrons
rows.operation_detail: Trained MNIST multilayer perceptrons with Adam using tanh, ReLU, or proposed activation functions and their paired initialization setup.
rows.value: For narrow networks (nl = 3), the proposed ϕθ functions generally decrease loss faster and attain better optima than tanh or ReLU; figure-only values.
rows.uncertainty: Training curves averaged over 5 experiments; no error bars stated.
rows.note: The text describes the aggregate comparison for the narrow-network setting; curves vary across depths and activation parameters. Activation and initialization are paired, so their separate contributions are not established.
rows.check: The reported aggregate advantage concerns odd activations with symmetric Weibull initialization, particularly width 3. It does not apply uniformly across parameters. Remove V3. Add the training-loss scheduler and validation-based early stopping; 0.001 is the initial learning rate.

source_check.locator_found: Section 5 introduction; Section 5.4, pp. 27–29, Figure 10; Appendix H.5.

rows.subject: multilayer perceptrons
rows.operation_detail: Trained MNIST multilayer perceptrons with ReLU and measured training loss.
rows.value: Training a narrow and deep neural network with a ReLU activation function is challenging; figure-only values.
rows.uncertainty: Training curves averaged over 5 experiments; no error bars stated.
rows.note: The authors explicitly describe ReLU training as challenging in narrow, deep networks. The text does not quantify the loss or give a training-error measure.
rows.check: Difficulty training narrow, deep ReLU perceptrons does not measure V3's specified convolutional-network comparison. This row also supplies no initialization contrast establishing V4's effect.

rows.subject: LeNet-type networks
rows.operation_detail: Trained CIFAR-10 LeNet-type networks with tanh, ReLU, or proposed activation functions and their paired initialization setup.
rows.value: ReLU and tanh perform well, along with some proposed functions; figure-only values.
rows.note: Authors describe several setups as performing well, but this is a loss-curve comparison rather than a reported training classification-error result.
rows.check: The activation and initialization comparison is relevant to V4, but 'perform well' establishes neither faster training nor greater trainable depth. Remove V3: architectures vary in width, with fixed depth and no shortcut comparison. The main figure concerns odd activations; some small-theta configurations perform well. Add the scheduler and validation-based early stopping.

relationships.condition: MNIST perceptrons of width 3 using odd activation and symmetric Weibull initialization pairs
relationships.reason: R1 reports generally faster loss reduction and better attained optima than tanh or ReLU with Gaussian EOC initialization; this supports the paired recipe's training benefit.
relationships.display_finding: The paired activation and initialization generally reduced loss faster and attained better optima than tanh or ReLU with Gaussian edge-of-chaos initialization.
